Abstract
Background This study aims to develop a fall risk perception toolkit based on “digital human” (FRP-digital human), 
test its usability among community-dwelling older patients with stroke, and verify its implementation effect.
Methods The toolkit underwent three phases: development, usability test, and effectiveness verification. A mixed 
method usability test was conducted with 20 participants who met the criteria. The toolkit was validated in a 12-week 
two-arm pilot study involving 80 community-dwelling older patients with stroke. Two groups of participants were 
randomly assigned to either the intervention or the control group to receive the same content of health education. 
Intervention group received health education based on “digital human”, while control group received traditional 
online PDF text health education. The usability test contained Post-Study System Usability Questionnaire (PSSUQ),

Customer Effort Score (CES), Net Promoter Score (NPS), and user interviews. Rate of Participant (RP), Rate of Adherence 
(RA), fall risk perception, object fall risk and quality of life were selected as outcome indicators. The corresponding 
measurement tools were calculation of RP and RA, Fall Risk Perception Scale for community-dwelling older adults 
(FRPS), Timed Up and Go test (TUG), and the Short Version of the Stroke Specific Quality of Life scale (SV-SS-QoL).
Results Four functional modules of FRP-digital human were determined. 20 participants completed the usability 
test. The CES was 3.1, NPS was 4.5 and the overall satisfaction of PSSUQ was 72.14%. Six themes were obtained from 
user interviews. A total of 80 participants completed the pilot study. The RP was 100% in both intervention group and 
control group, and significant differences was observed in RA between two groups (P<0.05). There were statistically 
significant differences in FRPS and the SV-SS-QoL between two groups (P<0.001). No statistically significant was 
observed in TUG between two groups (P=0.996).
Conclusion FRP-digital human can be accepted by community-dwelling older patients with stroke and help 
improve their fall risk perception and quality of life. Moreover, the design of the WeChat mini program increased its 
generalizability to promote more successful health care delivery.
Fall risk perception toolkit based on “digital 
human” for community-dwelling older 
patients with stroke: development 
and validation
Jiang Nan1 , Yi Hou1 , Manyao Sun1 , Xueying Huang1 , Jing Gao1 , Xueqiong Zou1 , Zhongyi Chen2 and 
Yuyu Jiang1*
Nan et al. BMC Geriatrics (2025) 25:532 Page 2 of 11
Introduction
Older patients with stroke often require home-based 
rehabilitation following hospital discharge. However, this 
population faces a significantly higher risk of falls compared to other groups, primarily due to decreased muscle strength and impaired balance function [1–4]. This 
increased fall risk not only compromises their quality of

life [5, 6] but also imposes a substantial burden on healthcare expenditures [7]. Global guidelines underscore 
the necessity of addressing fall risk perception (FRP) as 
a strategy to prevent falls [8]. FRP is defined as an individual’s cognitive process of first assessing their likelihood of falling and then determining the seriousness of 
that risk [9]. Enhancing FRP has been shown to improve 
older adults’ awareness of fall risks, promote behavioral 
changes [10], and reduce fall incidence [11].
Current FRP interventions are primarily delivered 
through models [12], graphics [13], and videos [14]. 
However, their reach and effectiveness remain limited 
[15]. With advancements in technology, digital interventions offer a promising solution to these challenges. 
Money et al. [16] have demonstrated that 3D serious 
games can serve as effective tools for health education 
among older adults. Nevertheless, tailoring fall prevention information to individual needs remains a challenge 
due to variability among recipients [17].
A “digital human”—a computer-generated virtual agent 
designed to emulate human behavior and personality 
traits—represents an innovative approach to enhance 
personalization in health interventions [18]. Despite this 
potential, previous studies have frequently neglected the 
integration of health beliefs into intervention design. 
Health beliefs play a pivotal role in fostering healthy 
behaviors and in empowering individuals to manage 
their health and well-being [19–21]. The incorporation of health beliefs into telemedicine frameworks has 
been shown to improve healthcare service delivery [22]. 
In China, WeChat is the most widely used social media 
platform among older adults. The development of digital 
health tools leveraging WeChat mini-programs—known 
for their low operational costs and ease of use—has the 
potential to significantly improve access to and utilization of healthcare services [23, 24].
The objective of this study is to develop a Fall Risk Perception Toolkit based on a “Digital Human” (FRP-digital 
human) for the intervention of FRP among communitydwelling older patients with stroke. This initiative aimed 
to expand the current intervention strategies targeting

FRP. A mixed-methods approach was employed to evaluate the toolkit’s usability and implementation efficacy. 
The development process was informed by the Health 
Belief Model [25] and the Double Diamond Model [26].
Methods
Study design, setting, and participants
This study was conducted in three phases: development, 
usability test, and effectiveness verification (the latter 
through a 12-week, two-arm pilot randomized controlled 
trial). Ethical approval was obtained from the institutional Medical Ethics Committee (JNU202212011RB24), 
and the study was registered with the Clinical Trials Registry. The CONSORT checklist is provided in the Supplemental Material.
Participant recruitment occurred between March 2023 
and May 2023. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) 
age≥65 years and residence in the community for ≥1 
year; (2) a first diagnosis of ischemic stroke confirmed 
via head CT or MRI (in accordance with the diagnostic criteria established by the Fourth Chinese Society of 
Cerebrovascular Disease); (3) ability to use WeChat and 
mini programs, either independently or after unified 
training; and (4) capacity for effective communication 
and completion of questionnaires, either independently 
or with researcher assistance. Exclusion criteria included: 
(1) activities of daily living (ADL) score<60, precluding 
gait data collection; (2) history of myocardial infarction, 
angina pectoris, or severe cardiac, hepatic, or renal disease within the past year; (3) excessive physical frailty 
preventing muscle strength testing; (4) cognitive or psychiatric impairment; and (5) history of syncope following 
physical exertion.
Sample size
Assuming a two-tailed alpha level of 0.05, 80% statistical power, and a 1:1 allocation ratio, Teare et al. [27] 
recommended a pilot sample size of 70 to reduce variability in standard deviation estimation. Whitehead et 
al. [28] further suggested that for standardized effect 
sizes between 0.2 and 0.5, a sample size of 32 to 92

participants is appropriate, using the non-central 
t-distribution approach. Additionally, they proposed 
a stepped rule of thumb, recommending a sample size 
of 50 when the standardized effect size is particularly 
small (δ < 0.1). Based on these considerations, a sample 
size of 92 was determined to adequately detect meaningful differences.
Trial registration This study has been registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry: ChiCTR2300068365 
(2023-02-16).
Keywords Fall risk perception, Digital intervention, Digital human, Home-based rehabilitation, Personalized 
healthcare, Older adults, Stroke

Randomization and blinding
Group assignments were concealed from assessors, 
intervention personnel (IP), and data analysts. Following 
completion of the baseline assessment, eligible participants were randomized into either the control or intervention group in a 1:1 ratio. The randomization sequence 
was generated using a computer-based random number 
generator and was managed by an independent research 
assistant who had no involvement in participant recruitment, data collection, or intervention implementation. 
This assistant maintained the randomization list and 
ensured its confidentiality. Upon group assignment, the 
results were transmitted via text message to assessors 
and intervention personnel by blinded research assistants. This procedure was implemented to minimize 
bias and uphold the integrity of the study. Details of the 
intervention protocol are presented in Table 1, with further information provided in the Supplemental Material.
Outcome measures
Usability test
The Post-Study System Usability Questionnaire (PSSUQ) 
[29] was employed to assess participant satisfaction. 
This instrument uses a Likert scale (e.g., 1 to 7), where 
higher scores indicate greater satisfaction. The Net Promoter Score (NPS) [30] was used to evaluate participants’ 
intention to recommend the toolkit. Responses were 
rated on a scale of 0 to 10, with scores of 0–6 classified

as “Detractors,” 7–8 as “Passives,” and 9–10 as “Promoters.” The NPS was calculated as follows: (number of Promoters−number of Detractors)/total sample size. The 
Customer Effort Score (CES) [31] was utilized to assess 
the effort required from participants. CES was rated on

number of participants. Additional user experience data 
were collected through individual interviews.
Effectiveness verification
The intervention comprised a total of 22 sessions. The 
participation rate (RP) was defined as the percentage of 
patients who completed all 22 sessions. Following each 
session, patients were required to answer questions 
pertaining to the session content; the adherence rate 
(RA) was calculated as the percentage of patients who

responded to these questions. The primary outcome of 
this study was FRP, measured using the Fall Risk Perception Scale for Community-Dwelling Older Adults (FRPS) 
[32]. This instrument encompasses three dimensions, 
with scores ranging from 0 to 68, where higher scores 
indicate greater fall risk perception among communitydwelling older adults. The Cronbach’s α coefficient for the 
scale is 0.913.
Secondary outcomes included objective fall risk and 
quality of life. Fall risk was assessed using the Timed Up 
and Go Test (TUG), where a duration of 13.5 s or more 
was indicative of increased fall risk [33]. Quality of life 
was evaluated using the Short Version of the Stroke-Specific Quality of Life Scale (SV-SS-QoL) [34], which comprises 12 items across three domains. Total scores range 
from 12 to 60, with higher scores reflecting better quality 
of life in stroke patients. The Cronbach’s α coefficient for 
this scale is 0.882.
Data collection
During the usability testing phase, data were collected 
in a home simulation laboratory. In the validation phase, 
demographic information and baseline outcome measures were collected from participants prior to the first 
intervention session. All outcome measures were reassessed three months following the intervention.
Data analysis
Data were analyzed using SPSS Statistics software (version 25.0, IBM Corp.), with statistical significance set at 
p<0.05. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize 
demographic and baseline characteristics. For normally 
distributed data, paired sample t-tests (within-group 
comparisons) and independent sample t-tests (betweengroup comparisons) were employed. For non-normally 
distributed data, the Mann–Whitney U test (withingroup comparisons) or the Wilcoxon rank-sum test 
(between-group comparisons) was applied.
Results
Phase 1: development of the FRP-digital human
The development of the FRP-digital human was guided 
by the Double Diamond Model and implemented 
through a WeChat mini program. The toolkit included 
four core functional modules: Digital Self, Knowledge 
Learning, Virtual Experience, and Help and Support.

In the “Virtual Experience” module, seven scenarios—
five indoor and two outdoor—were constructed based on 
the “Home Safety Checklist, CDC” [35], each incorporating structured fall risk factors. Participants could access 
personalized data via the “Digital Self” module and 
explore fall-related information through the “Knowledge 
Learning” module. A distinctive feature of the “Digital 
Self” module was the “Health Signature,” which visualized participants’ health beliefs and aimed to reinforce 
health-promoting behaviors through ongoing perceptual 
training.
The “Virtual Experience” module offered two functions: “Experience” and “Test.” The “Experience” function enabled the digital human to navigate life scenarios, 
simulating falls and injuries (e.g., bleeding or fractures of 
the limbs) when risk factors were not correctly identified. 
The “Test” function required the completion of two predefined tasks per scenario, which were designed based on 
the Instrumental Activities of Daily Living scale [36] to 
reflect daily functional requirements.
The “Help and Support” module provided feedback and 
professional guidance to participants. Version 1 of the 
FRP-digital human was finalized in this phase, and additional development details are provided in the Supplemental Material.
Phase 2: usability test of the FRP-digital human
In this phase, the finalized toolkit was tested for usability using a mixed-methods approach to evaluate effectiveness, efficiency, and user satisfaction, and to support 
iterative improvement. Participant experiences were captured through user interviews. Usability test followed the 
Common Industry Format for Usability Test Reports [37] 
issued by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, as detailed in the Supplemental Material.
A total of 20 eligible participants were selected via convenience sampling to complete core tasks—information 
viewing, knowledge learning, situational experience, and 
test evaluation—designed by the research team.
Effectiveness was assessed using the task completion 
rate, while efficiency was evaluated based on task completion time and the CES. Satisfaction was measured 
using the PSSUQ and the NPS. The results are presented 
in Table 2.

Six themes emerged from user interviews: (1) Preventive behaviors adopted post-intervention; (2) Digital human perceived as engaging and approachable; (3) 
Content deemed appropriate and conducive to effective 
learning; (4) Simple and user-friendly interface promoting ease of adoption; (5) Willingness to recommend the 
tool to others; (6) Overall positive user experience.

Phase 3: effectiveness verification of the FRP-Digital 
human
Recruitment process
The CONSORT flowchart is presented in Fig. 2. A total of 
145 patients were screened, of whom 92 (response rate: 
63%) met the eligibility criteria and agreed to participate. 
During the study, 12 participants withdrew, resulting in a 
dropout rate of 13%.

Baseline characteristics of participants
Baseline characteristics—including sociodemographic 
variables and outcome measures—were recorded for 
both the control and intervention groups. No statistically 
significant differences were observed between the two 
groups at baseline (p>0.05), as shown in Table 3.
Participant outcomes

Outcome measures included the RP, RA, FRPS, TUG, 
and the Short Version of the SV-SS-QoL. The results are 
presented in Table 4.
The RP was 100%, as all participants completed the 
22-session intervention. The RA in the intervention 
group was significantly higher than in the control group 
(t=4.528, P=0.029).
Regarding the FRPS, both groups exhibited improvement; however, the intervention group demonstrated 
a significantly greater improvement compared to the 
control group. Statistically significant differences were 
observed within both groups (Control group: t = −9.500, 
P<0.001; Intervention group: t = −15.555, P<0.001) as 
well as between groups (t = −10.09, P<0.001).
For the TUG, no statistically significant differences 
were found either within the groups (Control group: 
Z = −1.176, P=0.239; Intervention group: Z = −1.801, 
P=0.072) or between the groups (Z = −0.005, P=0.996).
In terms of the SV-SS-QoL, both groups showed 
improvements, with the intervention group achieving significantly higher improvements compared to the 
control group. Statistically significant differences were 
observed within both groups (Control group: t = −5.737, 
P<0.001; Intervention group: t = −6.912, P<0.001) as 
well as between groups (t = −17.254, P<0.001).
Discussion
This study indicated the digital human was not only 
well-accepted and utilized by older adults but also succeeded in providing personalized experiential engagement. Health beliefs shaped by personal experience may 
lead to innovative approaches in fall prevention. The display of individualized information via the digital human 
enhanced the degree of personalization, which is a critical factor in effective educational interventions [16, 38]. 
Compared with conventional display formats, the digital human exhibited greater dynamism and interactivity

[39], thereby enhancing educational engagement and 
comprehension [19]. Indeed, digital human technology has been applied within the healthcare domain as 
a form of digital twin. A digital twin integrates real and 
virtual components using measured data [40]. Previous 
research has primarily focused on constructing digital 
twins of patients to support healthcare professionals in 
building predictive models through machine learning 
[41]. Digital twin technology has also been employed 
to personalize interventions, such as in headache care 
[42]. However, in most prior studies, healthcare professionals were the primary users. In contrast, this study 
developed a digital human based on individual patient 
data for direct patient use. Participants were able to 
control the digital human within virtual environments, 
repeatedly experiencing the process of walking and falling to accumulate simulated “falling experiences.” Thiamwong [43] emphasized that fall prevention strategies 
for older adults are often informed by personal experience. Individual experiences can influence knowledge 
and attitudes, thereby altering health beliefs. The experience of falling or avoiding a fall can impact patients’ 
beliefs regarding fall prevention. Huang et al. [44] similarly suggested that fall prevention strategies should not 
adopt a one-size-fits-all approach; rather, older adults 
need exposure to diverse risk scenarios to maintain 
their quality of life. However, providing such experiential learning poses a challenge—namely, how to simulate falling experiences without causing physical harm. 
Although virtual reality has been employed in fall prevention interventions, its widespread implementation 
is limited by high equipment costs, lack of personalized 
data presentation, and the risk of injury during physically engaging programs. The digital human presents 
a feasible alternative to address these challenges. In 
this study, a safe virtual environment was established, 
enabling older adults to explore their physical limitations, adapt to discrepancies between perceived and 
actual fall risk, and proactively engage in fall prevention.
Psychological improvement precedes behavioral

change: autonomy as the critical bridge. Individual 
autonomy represents a crucial and indispensable factor linking FRP to fall-preventive behavior. The pilot 
study revealed that enhancing FRP among older stroke 
patients has the potential to improve their quality of 
life. Digital human intervention effectively improved 
FRP, consistent with the findings of Money et al. [16], 
who, although not using digital humans, employed a 
3D serious game to demonstrate the value of interactive exploration in improving FRP. However, this study 
did not observe statistically significant improvements 
in TUG scores (an indicator of objective fall risk), 
which contrasts with previous findings. This discrepancy may be explained by the study’s specific focus: it 
aimed solely to enhance FRP through innovative health 
education methods, rather than integrating exercisebased interventions whose benefits are well-established. Therefore, future research should incorporate 
physical activity components to promote improvements in physical function. This study aligns with the 
findings of Brouwer et al. [45], who reported improved 
quality of life following FRP interventions. The digital 
human likely contributed to this outcome by offering 
a personalized and interactive experience. Guided by 
the Health Belief Model, the digital human encouraged 
patients to adopt proactive health behaviors, thereby 
enhancing their quality of life. Despite demonstrated 
improvements in outcome measures, the underlying 
mechanisms through which FRP influences fall-prevention behavior remain insufficiently understood. 
Autonomy may be central to this mechanism. Robson 
et al. [46] proposed that autonomy is fundamental to 
decision-making among older adults. According to 
Self-Determination Theory [47], fulfillment of psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and 
relatedness generates intrinsic motivation and facilitates behavioral change. In this study, older adults 
completed tasks of varying difficulty through the

digital human, thereby building a sense of competence. 
Simultaneously, they operated within an autonomysupportive environment—freely navigating virtual scenarios with the digital human—which met their need 
for autonomy. On this basis, the following scientific 
hypothesis may be proposed: FRP influences autonomy, autonomy enhances behavioral motivation, and 
behavioral motivation drives behavioral change. This 
hypothesis may help explain how older adults can be 
effectively engaged in, and adhere to, fall-prevention 
interventions. Future studies should investigate and 
validate this potential mechanism. Additionally, the 
findings suggest that changes in risk perception may 
precede observable improvements in physical function. FRP may increase prior to behavioral changes, 
and further time may be required for those behavioral 
changes to translate into measurable physical improvements. This may account for the observed enhancement in FRP without corresponding improvement in 
TUG scores. Once FRP is heightened, participants may 
begin to adopt preventive behaviors—such as higher 
adherence rates—yet sustained implementation over 
time is needed for these behavioral modifications to

result in improved physical functioning and a corresponding reduction in objective fall risk. Further 
investigation into these mechanisms could contribute 
to more effective health promotion strategies in fall 
prevention.
Smart patients will be crucial for emerging service models in telemedicine. In the context of proactive health, self-directed health management reflects 
patients’ sense of responsibility for their own health 
and transforms them into both producers and consumers within the healthcare system. The World Guidelines 
for Falls Prevention and Management for Older Adults: 
A Global Initiative [8] emphasize that the perception 
of fall risk warrants greater attention, advocating for 
older adults to be recognized as primarily responsible 
for managing their own fall risk. This aligns with the 
“people-oriented” healthcare model. As an emerging 
technology, digital humans offer a novel and engaging experience that captures patients’ interest. However, with the advancement of telemedicine, patient 
experience—particularly digital patient experience—
has become a critical factor. Enhanced user experience enables patients not only to engage more fully 
in healthcare services but also to take an active role 
in their reform, thereby evolving into so-called smart 
patients. Smart patients [48] demonstrate a heightened 
sense of health responsibility, which contributes to 
more effective chronic disease management, promotes 
active ageing and health, and allows for the full utilization of digital healthcare services. Whether designed 
for healthcare professionals or patients, digital twins 
ultimately aim to enhance patient care. Digital doctors can deliver expert medical guidance, while digital 
patients continuously monitor their health in real time. 
As noted by Zalake [49], digital twins of physicians have 
the potential to optimize time management, automate 
the delivery of repetitive information, and personalize 
care. However, the dissemination of misinformation 
remains a potential risk; thus, ensuring the accuracy 
and reliability of information necessitates rigorous quality control. Furthermore, the influence of this emerging service model on doctor-patient interactions—and 
its resulting psychological and behavioral effects on 
individuals—remains uncertain and requires further 
investigation.
Limitations
Despite the accessibility of the study sample through 
WeChat or after receiving basic guidance, the e-health 
literacy of older adults remained a significant limiting

factor. Another limitation of this study is the potential 
Hawthorne effect, which may have been induced by the 
novelty of the technology itself. Therefore, it is advisable 
to implement a preparatory training period to ensure 
that participants’ e-health literacy reaches a sufficient 
level prior to the intervention. Additionally, the lack of 
long-term follow-up data represents a critical limitation, 
particularly in evaluating the sustainability of improvements in fall risk perception and fall-related behaviors. 
At the same time, adding the physical function exercise 
component to the health education intervention, it would 
facilitate the observation of effects at an objective level 
(e.g., TUG).
Conclusion
In conclusion, the FRP–digital human intervention provided a feasible and acceptable innovative approach for 
fall prevention. As a pilot study within the perception–
behavioral fall prevention framework, this work lays 
a solid foundation for future large-scale clinical trials. 
Moreover, the intervention toolkit is user-friendly, easy 
to implement, and broadly accessible, rendering it particularly suitable for application in primary healthcare settings and community-based interventions.
